reading.title: Planning the presentation space
reading.text: An adult event team visits an empty fashion-show venue. The catwalk is the presentation platform; backstage is out of the audience's view. The front row is nearest the presentation area. A lighting rig holds lights, and the sound system supplies audio. A backdrop sits behind the presentation, while the stage is the performance area. Seating describes the audience places. The press area is assigned to reporting, and the VIP section is reserved for invited guests. Casting selects participants, fitting checks clothing fit, and rehearsal practices the presentation. Hair styling and makeup are preparation activities, not types of equipment. The team checks the venue plan and assigned roles. The vocabulary explains organization without prescribing a show's layout or judging anyone's appearance.

reading.title: Coordinating show preparations
reading.text: The team reviews a fictional event schedule. Dressing means putting on the assigned clothes. The lineup is the order of looks or participants, while choreography plans movement and music selection chooses the audio. Invitations ask guests to attend. Fashion Week names a series of fashion-industry events rather than one universally fixed date. Paris, Milan, New York and London are cities associated with major fashion events, but the team checks the actual organizer's schedule. A designer develops the collection. Brand, label, house and maison can refer to a fashion business in this context; label can also have other meanings. The team asks which detail needs further refinement. It does not infer a company's identity, an event date or a person's invitation status from a photograph.

reading.title: Comparing fashion reporting
reading.text: After the fictional show, a fashion editor selects material for publication. A photographer creates images, while a fashion blog and magazine are different publishing formats. A review evaluates the event; coverage is the broader reporting about it. Social media provides another distribution channel. An influencer may affect an audience's choices, but a large following is not proof of expertise or independence. Street style concerns clothing seen in everyday public settings, whereas red carpet refers to a formal event setting or its carpet. The class compares the purpose of each report and asks which claims need support. It does not invent quotations, ratings or endorsements. The lesson uses these words to discuss media choices rather than directs learners to follow a particular account or attend an event.
